> **What this case shows** — the [HRV-DFA case](../hrv-dfa-aging-fantasia/index.qmd) measured the
> *fractal* scaling of the heartbeat (α1) and its rise with age. The **Poincare plot** measures the
> same variability *geometrically*: plot each RR interval against the next, and the scatter's two
> axes are **SD1** (short-term, beat-to-beat variability — a parasympathetic proxy) and **SD2**
> (long-term variability). On a real 5-minute RR window `ecgHRVpoincare` reproduces an independent
> from-scratch numpy analytical closed-form **bit-for-bit** (max |diff| = **0**), and NeuroKit2's
> `hrv_nonlinear`: **SD1 bit-for-bit**, **SD2** up to a documented ~0.2 ms convention. And the
> finding: short-term HRV (SD1) is far higher in the **young** (**53.1 ms**) than the **old**
> (**35.3 ms**) — the geometric complement of the DFA aging result.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — for the geometry of heart-rate variability: `ecgHRVpoincare(rr)` → read `sd1`
(short-term/vagal) and `sd2` (long-term).
**Way of thinking** — SD1 and SD2 are the width and length of the RR-scatter cloud: SD1 across the
line of identity (how much consecutive beats differ), SD2 along it (the overall spread). SD1 tracks
the fast, vagally-mediated variability that fades with age and disease.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioECG::ecgHRVpoincare()`; the nonlinear-HRV geometric complement of
`ecgDFA()` (fractal scaling).
:::

## Proposition

On a real 5-minute RR window (Fantasia f1y01), `ecgHRVpoincare`'s SD1/SD2 reproduce an independent
numpy analytical closed-form bit-for-bit (max |diff| 0), NeuroKit2's SD1 bit-for-bit and its SD2 up
to a ~0.2 ms convention; and SD1 is higher in the young (53.1 ms) than the old (35.3 ms).

## Question & goal

**The question is geometric: how wide and how long is the heartbeat scatter — and does the
ecosystem compute the Poincare descriptors exactly, agreeing with an established HRV toolbox?** The
goal is a machine-precision validation against two independent references and a read of the
age-related change in short-term variability.

## Challenge & approach

SD1 has one universal definition (SDSD/√2); SD2 has two — the *analytical* closed-form
(SD2² = 2·SDNN² − ½·SDSD²) and the *geometric* paired-projection (the std of (RRₙ+RRₙ₊₁)/√2). The op
uses the closed-form; NeuroKit2 uses the paired projection. We validate the op against an
independent numpy of its own closed-form (bit-exact), confirm SD1 matches NeuroKit2 exactly, and
*identify* the SD2 gap by reproducing NeuroKit2's SD2 with an independent numpy paired projection.

```
RR (Fantasia f1y01, 5-min) → ecgHRVpoincare → SD1 = 54.3, SD2 = 81.5 ms
              vs independent numpy analytical closed-form → bit-exact (max |diff| 0)
              vs NeuroKit2 hrv_nonlinear                  → SD1 bit-for-bit; SD2 = paired projection (~0.2 ms)
```

## Data

**Fantasia Database (PhysioNet)**: subject **f1y01** (young healthy adult), the first **5-minute**
RR window (391 intervals — the Task Force short-term HRV window); the young-vs-old panel uses all
**10** subjects (5 young + 5 old) — the same git-tracked Fantasia RR the sibling
[HRV-DFA case](../hrv-dfa-aging-fantasia/index.qmd) uses. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the Poincare plot for f1y01 (each RR interval against the next); the red ellipse's minor and major axes are SD1 = 54.3 ms (short-term) and SD2 = 81.5 ms (long-term); ecgHRVpoincare equals an independent numpy analytical closed-form bit-for-bit, and its SD1 equals NeuroKit2's SD1 bit-for-bit. Right: Poincare SD1 across the 5 young and 5 old subjects — short-term HRV is markedly higher in the young (mean 53.1 ms) than the old (35.3 ms), an age-related decline in cardiac-vagal variability.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the left panel is the geometry (SD1/SD2 = the cloud's width/length) and the
validation (op = numpy exactly, SD1 = NeuroKit2 exactly); the right panel is the finding (SD1 falls
with age).

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| **SD1 (short-term, f1y01)** | **54.3 ms** |
| **SD2 (long-term, f1y01)** | **81.5 ms** |
| SD1/SD2 ratio | **0.67** |
| op vs independent numpy closed-form (max \|diff\|) | **0** (bit-exact) |
| op SD1 vs NeuroKit2 SD1 | **0** (bit-exact) |
| numpy paired-projection vs NeuroKit2 SD2 | **0** (identifies the convention) |
| op SD2 vs NeuroKit2 SD2 (convention gap) | **0.20 ms** (~0.24%) |
| **young mean SD1 → old mean SD1** | **53.1 → 35.3 ms** |

The op matches an independent numpy closed-form and NeuroKit2's SD1 to the bit; the SD2 difference
is a resolved convention, not an error; and short-term HRV declines with age. Values trace to
[`artifacts/poincare_summary.csv`](artifacts/poincare_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

The ecosystem's Poincare descriptors are the exact analytical SD1/SD2 — bit-for-bit against
independent numpy, and bit-for-bit against NeuroKit2 for the universally-defined SD1 — and on real
RR they measure the age-related fall in short-term, vagally-mediated variability, the geometric
complement of the DFA fractal-aging result on the same cohort. The transferable takeaway: **SD1 is
the beat-to-beat (parasympathetic) axis and SD2 the long-term axis; SD1 has one definition but SD2
has two (analytical closed-form vs geometric paired projection) that differ at O(1/n) — know which
your toolbox reports before you compare across tools.**

## Open questions

- The op reports the standard SD1/SD2; the full Poincare literature adds the temporal-asymmetry
  indices (Guzik / Porta) that separate heart-rate *decelerations* from *accelerations*. Computing
  the asymmetry across the young/old cohort — and pairing it with the DFA α1 on the same beats —
  would test whether the geometric and fractal aging signatures track the same autonomic change.
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Poincare SD1/SD2 (nonlinear HRV geometry) | `ecgHRVpoincare()` | PhysioECG |
| fractal scaling α1/α2 (the complement) | `ecgDFA()` | PhysioECG |
| RR intervals from an ECG | `ecgRRintervals()` | PhysioECG |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **the window** — SD1/SD2 are usually read on the 5-minute short-term HRV window (Task Force 1996);
  a longer recording mixes circadian drift into SD2.
- **SD1 vs SD2** — SD1 (short-term) is the vagal/parasympathetic axis that falls with age, disease,
  and stress; SD2 (long-term) tracks the overall spread and the sympatho-vagal balance.
- **the SD2 convention** — the op reports the analytical closed-form; a paired-projection toolbox
  (e.g. NeuroKit2) differs at O(1/n). For 5-min windows the gap is ~0.2 ms (negligible), but pin the
  convention before cross-tool comparison.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioECG)

p <- ecgHRVpoincare(rr)   # rr: data.frame(channel, rr_ms, time_sec)
p$sd1   # 54.3 ms -- short-term (beat-to-beat, parasympathetic) variability
p$sd2   # 81.5 ms -- long-term variability

# reproduces an independent numpy analytical closed-form bit-for-bit (max |diff| 0);
# SD1 matches NeuroKit2 bit-for-bit; SD2 up to a ~0.2 ms paired-projection convention.
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/poincare_summary.csv`](artifacts/poincare_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py)
re-checks each number, the three bit-exact identities (op = numpy, op SD1 = NeuroKit2 SD1, numpy
paired projection = NeuroKit2 SD2), the resolved SD2 convention, the aging finding, and the
honestly-noted scope.
